extracted.intended_audience: general encyclopedia readers and those interested in scientific integrity, research misconduct, and publication ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating scientific publications for inappropriate image duplication, manipulation, and related research-misconduct indicators; and assessing journal/editorial responses (corrections, retractions, screening).

rubrics_metrics.name: Image duplication and manipulation in figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Duplicated images and manipulated panels (e.g., panels representing different experimental conditions but showing identical or altered images) in scientific publications constitute inappropriate image duplication and are a key indicator of problematic data presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples on the page show duplicated panels highlighted; some duplications may be "honest errors during assembly of the figures", while others are intentional. Investigations may lead to corrections or retractions depending on severity and intent. Community posting (e.g., on Twitter, PubPeer) is used to flag suspect images for further scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevalence and quantification of problematic images
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative measures reported (from Bik and coauthors' studies) — e.g., nearly 400 papers with intentional figure manipulation (~800 duplicate images); in one journal analysis 59 of 960 papers (6.1%) contained inappropriately duplicated images; a pilot image screening program found problems with 14.5% of subsequent submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prevalence statistics to justify screening programs and to assess scope of the problem. Reported percentages help journals and institutions prioritize interventions and resources for image checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing honest errors from intentional misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Some duplicated or altered images may result from honest assembly errors, whereas others reflect intentional attempts to mislead; intent influences corrective action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations should consider context, patterns across multiple figures/papers, and admissions by authors. Outcomes have included corrections (for honest/less-severe cases) and retractions (for serious or intentional manipulation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction vs retraction decision criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial responses vary: examples include 41 papers with corrections published and 5 papers retracted in one analysis; severity, intent, and impact on conclusions influence whether a correction or a retraction is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should evaluate whether duplicated/manipulated images invalidate results or conclusions, whether authors admit wrongdoing, and whether policies on publishing ethics warrant retraction versus issuing a correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial and publisher standards for clinical research reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Clinical trial reports must meet publisher/society expected standards, including justified criteria for patient selection and triage, adherence to publishing ethics policies, and appropriate conduct of research involving human participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of justification for inclusion criteria or triage and failures in human-subjects conduct can prompt publishers to admit the article did not meet standards and to commission independent evaluations, possibly leading to retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest disclosure and assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Undisclosed or problematic conflicts of interest in authors or editors (e.g., relationships between authors and editorial staff) are grounds for concern about the integrity of a publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should manage and disclose conflicts (e.g., recusal of editors), and independent evaluation may be required if conflicts are alleged to have influenced publication decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review and editorial process integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: The integrity and transparency of peer review and editorial decision-making are criteria for assessing a publication's trustworthiness (e.g., whether an editor participated in evaluation, whether peer review was adequate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If standard peer-review safeguards are compromised or questioned, journals may perform additional independent evaluations and issue editorial notes while investigations proceed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-publication image screening as a quality-control measure
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic image screening by journals or editorial offices can detect problematic figures before publication (pilot programs reported identifying ~14.5% problematic submissions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementing automated or manual image checks as part of submission processing can reduce the incidence of problematic images in the literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection of paper mills and patterned fabrication
rubrics_metrics.description: Clusters of papers with similar problematic features (e.g., originating from the same 'paper mill') are indicators of fabricated research; investigations identified over 400 dubious papers apparently from the same production company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for repetitive patterns, near-duplicate content, and coordinated production signatures across papers to identify possible paper-mill output and mobilize corrective actions (notices, retractions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Emerging threat: AI-generated fraudulent images
rubrics_metrics.description: Artificial intelligence can be used to fraudulently generate scientific images (e.g., Western blots), representing a new avenue for data fabrication and manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Awareness and development of detection approaches are necessary; researchers, editors, and conferences should consider the risk of AI-generated falsified images and update screening methods accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of post-publication review and community scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-publication platforms (e.g., PubPeer, Retraction Watch) and social media are instrumental for reporting, publicizing, and investigating potential image problems and other misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Community-led scrutiny can prompt journal investigations, corrections, retractions, and broader policy responses; contributors may face pushback or legal threats, so supportive institutional responses (open letters, petitions) and protections for whistleblowers are important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional and community responses to harassment/legal threats
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists and defenders of integrity who flag problems may face legal action or harassment (example: legal threats against Bik), prompting collective actions such as open letters, petitions, and calls for authorities to intervene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholarly societies and the scientific community may issue public support, and institutions should consider mechanisms to protect and support post-publication reviewers and whistleblowers.
